explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says Jehoiachin "did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as his father had done" (2 Kings 24:9). His father was Jehoiakim, the king before him. Three months on the throne, and the writer still has that much to say about it.

Not quite, friend. The text says Jehoiachin "did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as his father had done" (2 Kings 24:9). His father was Jehoiakim, the king before him. So the son followed the same path, and this one doesn't need a second look.

That's it, baker. The servants of Nebuchadnezzar marched up to Jerusalem, "and the city came under siege" (2 Kings 24:10). A siege means the city gets surrounded and shut in. Nobody's popping out for errands.

explanations.answer: It pays them to go home
explanations.explanation: I get the hope, friend, but the text never mentions a payment. It says the servants of Nebuchadnezzar marched up and "the city came under siege" (2 Kings 24:10). They didn't leave, and they weren't talked out of it. They set up around the walls.

explanations.answer: It sends out its army to fight
explanations.explanation: That sounds brave, friend, but the text doesn't say it. What it says is "the city came under siege" (2 Kings 24:10). So Jerusalem is shut in, with Nebuchadnezzar's servants around it. No battle charge shows up in these verses.

explanations.answer: He surrenders to the king of Babylon
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Jehoiachin, his mother, his servants, his commanders and his officials "all surrendered to the king of Babylon" (2 Kings 24:12). He didn't hold out. I think that took some nerve of its own, handing it all over with the king standing right there.

explanations.answer: He sneaks out of the city at night
explanations.explanation: Nice sneaky guess, friend, but that's not in this passage. The text says Jehoiachin and his people "all surrendered to the king of Babylon" (2 Kings 24:12). No midnight exit, no tiptoeing past the guards. He gave himself up.

explanations.answer: He rides out to fight the king of Babylon
explanations.explanation: That would make a big scene, friend, but it isn't what happened. Jehoiachin, his mother, his servants, his commanders and his officials "all surrendered to the king of Babylon" (2 Kings 24:12). No charge, no battle. They surrendered.

Careful, friend, because the text says otherwise. Jehoiachin "his mother, his servants, his commanders, and his officials all surrendered to the king of Babylon" (2 Kings 24:12). He wasn't a one-man surrender. The whole group went together.

That's right, baker. The text says "Jehoiachin king of Judah, his mother, his servants, his commanders, and his officials all surrendered to the king of Babylon" (2 Kings 24:12). The whole group gave themselves up together. Nobody stayed out of it.
Not this time, friend. The text says Nebuchadnezzar "carried off all the treasures from the house of the LORD and the royal palace" (2 Kings 24:13). Nothing stayed where it was. He took them away.
Right, baker. Nebuchadnezzar "carried off all the treasures from the house of the LORD and the royal palace" (2 Kings 24:13). Both places were emptied. Not one thing was left sitting on the shelf.

Yes, baker. The text says Nebuchadnezzar "cut into pieces all the gold articles that Solomon king of Israel had made in the temple of the LORD" (2 Kings 24:13). Those were made long before, in Solomon's day. That's a hard thing to read, and I think it stings.

explanations.answer: He leaves them in the temple
explanations.explanation: I wish it went that way, friend, but it doesn't. Nebuchadnezzar "cut into pieces all the gold articles that Solomon king of Israel had made in the temple of the LORD" (2 Kings 24:13). Solomon was Israel's king long before this. His gold articles didn't stay put.

explanations.answer: He hands them to his servants
explanations.explanation: Good guess, friend, but the text goes another way. Nebuchadnezzar "cut into pieces all the gold articles that Solomon king of Israel had made in the temple of the LORD" (2 Kings 24:13). Solomon was Israel's king long ago. There's no handing out here. The pieces were cut.

That's the one, baker. The text says "Only the poorest people of the land remained" (2 Kings 24:14). The commanders, the mighty men, the craftsmen and the metalsmiths were all taken. The poorest were left behind in the land.

Close to something that sounds sensible, friend, but the text says "poorest." It reads, "Only the poorest people of the land remained" (2 Kings 24:14). Age isn't what the verse talks about here. The ones left were the poorest.
Good try, friend, but that word isn't in the verse. The text says "Only the poorest people of the land remained" (2 Kings 24:14). Nothing is said about age. The ones left behind were the poorest.

That's right, baker. Nebuchadnezzar carried Jehoiachin to Babylon "as well as the king's mother, his wives, his officials, and the leading men of the land" (2 Kings 24:15). The wives went too. It was the king's whole household.

Not quite, friend. The text says Nebuchadnezzar carried away Jehoiachin to Babylon "as well as the king's mother, his wives, his officials, and the leading men of the land" (2 Kings 24:15). So the wives were taken too. They're right there in the list.

You've got it, baker. The text says the seven thousand men of valor and the thousand craftsmen and metalsmiths were "all strong and fit for battle" (2 Kings 24:16). These were the people you'd count on. And Babylon took every one of them.

Nice thought, friend, but the verse says something else. These men were "all strong and fit for battle" (2 Kings 24:16). The word is battle, not farming. They were fighters and skilled workers, and they were carried off.
I see why you'd go there, friend, but the verse says otherwise. These men were "all strong and fit for battle" (2 Kings 24:16). Trading doesn't come up at all. The word is battle.

Not this time, friend. The text says "the king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's uncle, king in his place" (2 Kings 24:17). Egypt's king isn't part of this moment. It was Nebuchadnezzar's call.

That would be a fair way to do it, friend, but it isn't what happened. "The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's uncle, king in his place" (2 Kings 24:17). The leading men had already been carried off to Babylon (2 Kings 24:15). So the choice came from Babylon.
